1.pericope_label: A wise son heareth his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke... He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life... There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches. The ransom of a man's life are his riches

schools.summary: Ellicott offers on the first verse a construction none of the others entertain, that a wise son is his father's instruction, meaning the result and embodiment of it rather than the hearer of it. On the mouth he cross-refers to the neighbouring chapters without argument; on the pretended rich he compares the man who lays up treasure for himself and the counsel to sell what one has; and on the ransom he explains that in times of trouble the rich man may have to give all he has to save his life, while the poor man hears no threatening because he has no need to regard it, his poverty and insignificance being his protection. Delitzsch groups the chapter's opening for the reader: the first three proverbs refer to hearing and speaking, and a fourth follows which, like the second and third, speaks of the soul. He defends the Greek and Syriac rendering, a shrewd son obedient to his father, against the charge of having read a different Hebrew form, arguing that those translators correctly understood the text by the Jewish rule of interpretation that what is wanting is to be supplied from the context. Mouth and soul, he says, stand in the closest interchangeable relation, since speech is the most immediate and continuous expression of the soul; and on the ransom he corrects a scholar who understood the second clause of warning, since the contrast points rather to threatening with the loss of life.

Gill notices that the possessive is absent from the second verse, so that the fruit may be another's mouth or one's own, and reports the Greek and Arabic rendering, the fruits of righteousness. He has the man who keeps his mouth keep it as with a bridle, from speaking of others and particularly of those in high places, and so keep his life out of danger. On the sluggard he sets out the pattern: he desires knowledge but will not be at the pains to get it, desires riches but will not be diligent, desires good clothing but is unwilling to labour and is therefore clothed with rags. He hates lying as a word of falsehood contrary to honour, truth and conscience, and hates it in every kind, in common conversation, in religion, in doctrine, and spoken in hypocrisy. On the two pretences he describes men who make a great show of riches, put on fine clothes and live at a high rate to gratify pride and to draw others into trusting them with their substance, and finds the same thing done in religion by hypocrites who would be thought rich in grace and possessed of every grace of the Spirit while the root of the matter is not in them.

Clarke opens with a table of the chapter's contents before expounding a line of it: various moral sentences, the wise child, continence of speech, the poor rich man and the rich poor man, ill-gotten wealth, the delay of what is hoped for, the consequences of refusing instruction, providing for one's children and the necessity of correcting them. On the mouth he observes how often the foolish, headstrong and wicked have forfeited their lives by the treasonable or blasphemous words they have spoken, and that the government of the tongue is a rare but useful talent, while he who opens wide his lips puts no bounds to his loquacity and gives his opinion on every matter. He turns the sluggard inward, on religious people who express a desire for more of the divine life and never get forward, because they desire but do not stir themselves up to lay hold upon the Lord, always learning but never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. The two pretences he names sharply, the rich poor man and the poor rich man, illustrating the first from the fable of the dog in the manger and the second from the apostle who was as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing yet possessing all things; and on the ransom he notes that in despotic countries a rich man is often accused of some capital crime and must give up his riches to save his life though quite innocent, while the poor are put to no trouble. Wesley glosses briefly, that the man eats good by receiving comfort and benefit from his own wise and profitable discourses, and that riches enable a man to redeem his life when it is in greatest danger while poverty preserves a man from many injuries, both because the poor are cautious not to provoke others and because they are esteemed objects of pity.

Henry begins with the family: among the children of the same parents it is no new thing for some to be hopeful and others the contrary, and there is great hope of those who have a reverence for their parents and are willing to be advised by them. On the mouth he makes the guard on the lips a guard to the soul, wanting a man who is cautious, who thinks twice before he speaks once, who lays his hand on his mouth to suppress an evil thought if he has thought one, and who keeps a strong bridle on his tongue and a strict hand on that bridle. He catches the sluggard's absurdity in a sentence, that they desire the gains which the diligent get but hate the pains which the diligent take, coveting everything that is to be coveted while doing nothing that is to be done. Where grace reigns, he says, sin is loathsome, and it is the undoubted character of every righteous man that he hates lying, that is, all sin, since every sin is a lie, not merely that he will not tell one but that he abhors lying from a rooted and reigning principle of love to truth. On riches he warns that we are apt to judge men's blessedness by their wealth, and that Solomon shows what a gross mistake this is, so that we may be reconciled to a poor condition and neither covet riches ourselves nor envy those that have abundance.

debates.question: How is the first line to be construed?

positions.view: A wise son hears his father's instruction, asks for it and delights in it.
A wise son is his father's instruction, the result and embodiment of it.
The Greek and Syriac give a shrewd son obedient to his father, and are right to supply what the text leaves out.

debates.question: What does the sluggard's case teach?

positions.view: That he desires knowledge, riches and clothing without the pains of getting them, and so goes in rags.
That they desire the gains the diligent get but hate the pains the diligent take.
The same failure in religion: men desire more of the divine life but never stir themselves up to lay hold on the Lord.
The positive half: the soul of the industrious is richly satisfied.

debates.question: Who is better off in the verse about ransom?

positions.view: The poor, whose poverty and insignificance are his protection, so that he need not regard a threat.
The poor, since under despotic rule the rich are accused of capital crimes and must buy their lives though innocent.
The poor, being cautious not to provoke others and esteemed objects of pity.
Neither: we judge blessedness by wealth, and the verse shows what a gross mistake that is.

outliers.note: Defends the Greek and Syriac translators against the charge of having read a different Hebrew form, crediting them with a known Jewish rule of interpretation.
Prints a table of the chapter's contents before commenting on a single line of it.

themes: A wise son heareth his father’s instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke.
A man shall eat good by the fruit of his mouth: but the soul of the transgressors shall eat violence.
He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction.
The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.
A righteous man hateth lying: but a wicked man is loathsome, and cometh to shame.
Righteousness keepeth him that is upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner.
There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.
The ransom of a man’s life are his riches: but the poor heareth not rebuke.

9.pericope_label: The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out. Only by pride cometh contention... Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life... Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard

schools.summary: Ellicott draws a distinction between the light of the righteous and the lamp of the wicked: the one walks in the light of God's truth, so that his path becomes continually more plain, while the other walks by the glimmer of his own lamp; and the verb means that the light burns joyously, as the sun rejoices as a giant to run his course. On pride he renders the line that by pride cometh nothing but contention, since a man too proud to receive counsel is sure to fall out with others, while they are wise who suffer themselves to be advised. Wealth by vanity he glosses as gained in an unsatisfactory manner, that is, by dishonesty. On the word despised he allows two senses, that the despiser literally brings ruin on himself, or that he is still bound to the word even though he contemptuously neglect it, comparing the counsel to agree with an adversary quickly, that is, to satisfy the requirements of God's law while there is time. He prefers instruction to law in the fourteenth verse and traces the snares of death to the devil; and he makes the way of transgressors rough and barren as a valley named in the law, against the green pastures and waters of comfort of the psalm. Delitzsch notices formal links between the proverbs: three successive ones whose two concluding words correspond almost rhythmically, and a group of four whose connection appears to have been occasioned by the sound of their words. He restricts the particle in the pride verse to contention rather than to pride, renders the wealth verse that fraud always makes wealth less while labour always makes it more, takes the word despised as ordering and the despiser as in bonds to it, and observes that the figures of paradise in the twelfth and fourteenth verses require the verse between them to be taken along with both.

Gill takes the light of the righteous for the light of joy and gladness, of spiritual knowledge and experience, of sound doctrine and of good works, increasing more and more to the perfect day. On pride he offers an alternative rendering, that an empty man through pride will make contention, since those who are empty of knowledge and wisdom are generally the most proud. Wealth gotten by vanity he defines by its methods: robbery and theft, fraud and circumvention, cards and dice and stage playing, and the curious and illicit arts of necromancy and judiciary astrology. On hope deferred he has the mind grow uneasy and the heart sink and fail when the object hoped for is delayed, so that the man is dispirited and ready to despond. He takes the word despised for Christ himself, the essential Word, and finds the contempt in those who despise his ministers and the gospel they preach; the law of the wise he makes the doctrine of those taught by the word, a fountain of living water; good understanding gives favour among men and among the religious; and the wicked messenger falls from the degree of honour in which he stood, losing his master's favour and being degraded from his office.

Clarke reads both the light and the lamp as posterity, so that the righteous shall have a joyous posterity while that of the wicked shall be cut off. On pride he extends the principle as far as it will go: perhaps there is not a quarrel among individuals in private life, nor a war among nations, that does not proceed from pride and ambition, since neither man nor nation will be content to be less than another. Wealth not the result of honest industry is seldom permanent, and all fortunes acquired by speculation, by lucky hits, and by ministering to the pride or luxury of others soon become dissipated, not being gotten in the way of providence and having no blessing on them. His analysis of hope deferred is the fullest in the chapter: when a good is discovered, the want of it felt, strong desire for its possession excited, and the promise of attainment made on grounds unsuspected, hope posts forward to realise the blessing, and delay in the gratification pains the mind. On the law of the wise he would rather translate that the law is to the wise man a fountain of life, the same to him as the great artery which transmits the blood from the heart to every part of the body, with an allusion to the garden of paradise behind it. On the way of transgressors he writes the sharpest sentence in the chapter, that never was a truer saying, since most sinners have more pain and difficulty to get their souls damned than the righteous have, with all their cross-bearings, to get to the kingdom of heaven; and on the messenger he reports that the Greek read a bold king in place of a messenger, standing alone in that reading. Wesley glosses the light as prosperity whose end is hidden, says it is chiefly pride which blows up the coals of contention while the well-advised are governed not by their passions but by prudent considerations, calls the transgressor's way offensive and hateful to God and men as rough ways are to a traveller, and makes the faithful messenger procure benefit to his master and to himself.

Henry has the light of the righteous increase and make them glad, their outward prosperity being their joy and much more the gifts and graces with which their souls are illuminated, since the Spirit is their light and gives them a fulness of joy. Foolish pride he calls the great make-bate: would you know whence come wars and fightings, they come from this root of bitterness, and whatever hand other lusts may have in contention, whether passion or envy or covetousness, pride has the great hand, for it will itself sow discord and needs no help. Riches, he says, wear as they are won and woven, since that which is won ill will never wear well, a curse attending it, and the same corrupt dispositions which incline men to sinful ways of getting incline them to the like sinful ways of spending. On hope deferred he finds nothing more grievous than the disappointment of a raised expectation, not in the thing itself by a denial but in the time of it by a delay, since hope deferred makes the heart sick and languishing, fretful and peevish, while hope quite dashed kills the heart, and the higher the expectation was raised the more cutting is the frustration of it. He makes the despiser of the word marked for ruin, since he slights the only means of curing a destructive disease; and he counts it wisdom to be cautious, the prudent man doing all with knowledge, considering with himself and consulting with others, and careful not to meddle with what he has no knowledge of.

debates.question: What is the difference between the light of the righteous and the lamp of the wicked?

positions.view: The one walks in the light of God's truth, whose path grows plainer; the other by the glimmer of his own lamp.
Both terms mean posterity: the righteous shall have a joyous line, the wicked's shall be cut off.
The Spirit is their light, giving a fulness of joy beyond outward prosperity.
The light is prosperity, whose end for the wicked is hidden.

debates.question: How does the restrictive particle work in the verse on pride?

positions.view: It belongs to contention, not to pride: nothing comes by pride but contention.
The line may instead be read that an empty man through pride will make contention.

debates.question: What follows from despising the word?

positions.view: He is in bonds to it, the word being thought of as an ordering commandment.
Either he brings ruin on himself, or he remains bound to the word while contemptuously neglecting it.
The word is Christ himself, despised in those who despise his ministers.
Ruin, since the revelation despised is the only way of salvation there is.

outliers.note: Writes the chapter's most quotable line, that most sinners have more pain and difficulty to get their souls damned than the righteous have to reach heaven.
Twice groups the proverbs by the sound of their words rather than their sense, finding rhythmic correspondence and catchword linkage where the others see only maxims.

themes: The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out.
Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed: but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded.
The law of the wise is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death.
Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard.
Every prudent man dealeth with knowledge: but a fool layeth open his folly.
A wicked messenger falleth into mischief: but a faithful ambassador is health.

18.pericope_label: Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction... He that walketh with wise men shall be wise... He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes. The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his soul

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the verse on desire two constructions and lets both stand: either the fools' clinging to evil prevents them attaining objects worth desiring, or, if the particle be read as therefore, the sense is that because the satisfaction of desire is pleasant they will give up nothing, however evil, on which they have set their minds. He glosses the destruction of the fool's companion as moral ruin, sets the snares and fire and brimstone of one psalm against the good measure, pressed down and shaken together and running over, that awaits the righteous, and notices that the good man of the inheritance verse answers to the just man of the second line, so that the word probably means liberal or unselfish. The tillage he takes for newly made field on which much labour has been expended, so that the poor hardworking man gains an abundant living by God's blessing while many rich persons are ruined for their neglect of what is right; betimes he glosses as while the child may yet be influenced rightly, before faults are rooted in him. Delitzsch ranges these verses as two pairs about fools and wise men joined by catchwords, remarks that the verb of pursuit is used of a punishment which follows sinners at their heels and that Greek art gives wings to Nemesis in that sense, renders the second line of the company proverb that whoever has intercourse with fools becomes base, and denies that the closing verse is any commendation of temperance and moderation at all.

Gill carries the poverty and shame of the eighteenth verse into the next world as everlasting shame and contempt, and makes the desire accomplished cover both the lower objects, riches and honour and knowledge, and the highest, the knowledge of God and communion with him. On company he has the man who walks with the wise converse frequently with them in private about spiritual and experimental things and walk with them in public in all the commandments, growing wiser by both. Evil pursuing sinners he takes of a damnation which may seem to slumber and linger but does not, being upon the full speed after them and certain to overtake them. The inheritance he grounds on honesty, since what is got honestly wears well and is enjoyed not only by the immediate offspring but by theirs after them. On the rod he says that such fond love as spares it is no better than hatred, since a father who really hated his son could scarcely do him a worse turn than not to correct him for a fault, which was the sin of Eli; and the righteous man's eating he makes both a sufficiency and a contentment, since he has enough and eats no more than suffices, indulging neither luxury nor excess.

Clarke makes the proverb on company turn on affection: to walk with a person implies love and attachment, and it is impossible not to imitate those we love, so that we may say, show me his company and I will tell you the man, and let me know the company he keeps and I shall easily guess his moral character. The inheritance he makes partly immaterial, since the good man files many a prayer in heaven on his children's behalf and his good example and advices are remembered and quoted from generation to generation, while whatever property he left was honestly acquired and well-gotten goods are permanent, property ill-gotten seldom reaching to the third generation, as even the heathens observed. On the tillage he turns the second clause against the poor themselves, asking how much of the poverty of the poor arises from their own want of management, since they have little or no economy and no foresight, and when they get anything they speedily spend it, so that a feast and a famine make the chief varieties of their life. On the rod he says that if a father hated his son he could not do him a greater disservice than to leave him uncorrected when his obstinacy requires it, and quotes a writer who observes that by the neglect of early correction the passions obtain ascendancy. The last verse he reads as contentment: the righteous man's desires are all moderate and he is pleased with the lot God sends, while the wicked, though he use all shifts and expedients to acquire earthly good, not sticking even at rapine and wrong, is frequently in real want and always dissatisfied, so that a contented mind is a continual feast at which he never eats. Wesley notes that whatever men earnestly desire is sweet to them when enjoyed, which is why sinners rejoice in the satisfaction of their sinful lusts and abhor all restraint of them, that the evil pursuing sinners is punishment proportionable to their sin, that poor persons by their diligent labours and God's blessing often grow rich, and that a father's fond affection is as pernicious to a son as hatred.

Henry has the man who is so proud that he scorns to be taught refuse the good instruction offered him as if it were a reflection upon his honour and an abridgment of his liberty, and finds in the next verse the folly of such men, since they might be happy and will not. Those that would be good, he says, must keep good company, which is both an evidence that they would be good, men's character being known by the company they choose, and a means of making them so. On the pursuit of sinners he asks where they can go, since evil pursues them closely wherever they are, as the avenger of blood pursued the manslayer, and they have no city of refuge to flee to, for whom God pursues he is sure to overtake. He counts it part of a good man's praise that he is thoughtful for posterity and does not lay all out upon himself, not by withholding more than is meet but by a prudent and decent frugality; and he answers the excuse of a small estate, since much food is in the tillage of the poor who take pains with the little they have, and the less compass the field is of the more skill and industry it deserves. On correction he requires the rod of a parent, directed by wisdom and love and designed for good, not the rod of a servant, since every child of ours is a child of Adam and has that foolishness bound up in its heart which calls for rebuke; and he finds the happiness of the righteous in having enough and knowing when they have enough, since nature is content with a little and grace with less, and enough is as good as a feast.

debates.question: Who is blamed in the second half of the tillage verse?

positions.view: The rich, who are ruined for their neglect of what is right while the poor labourer prospers.
Those destroyed by iniquity, without narrowing it to a class.
The poor themselves, whose want of management and foresight makes a feast and a famine the chief varieties of their life.
Nobody in particular: the verse answers the excuse that a man has too little to work on.

debates.question: What is the good man's inheritance?

positions.view: The legacy of a liberal and unselfish man, answering to the just man of the second line.
Prayers filed in heaven and an example quoted from generation to generation, besides honestly acquired property.
The fruit of a prudent and decent frugality, in a man thoughtful for posterity.
What was got honestly and therefore wears well through more than one generation.

debates.question: What does the closing verse commend?

positions.view: Having enough and knowing when you have enough, since nature is content with a little and grace with less.
A contented mind, which is a continual feast at which the wicked never eats.
Neither temperance nor moderation; the verse commends nothing of the kind.
Simply that the righteous has enough for his wants.

outliers.note: Reads the tillage proverb against the poor, blaming their want of economy and foresight where the others blame the rich or leave the class unnamed.
Denies that the chapter's closing verse commends temperance at all, against every other voice's reading of it as contentment.

themes: Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured.
The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul: but it is abomination to fools to depart from evil.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repayed.
A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment.
He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his soul: but the belly of the wicked shall want.
